summary: Fe–30 at.% Al is a binary Fe–Al intermetallic alloy that was induction melted, drop cast and slowly cooled to a coarse-grained, weakly DO3-ordered (well B2-ordered) state, then deformed in room-temperature compression to a plastic strain of 2–3% for TEM study of the resulting dislocation substructure. This sample is one of the high-Al compositions (28–35% Al) in a systematic study of work hardening in polycrystalline Fe–Al alloys, where the work hardening rate passes through a sharp maximum near 26–30% Al; it is used to document how deformation in the ordered state proceeds by straight, near-screw superdislocations (pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials) that leave numerous edge dipoles, reaction-produced dislocation pairs and residual APBII fringes behind.
composition: Binary Fe–Al alloy with 30% Al (atomic percent is used throughout the paper). It is one of a series of binary Fe–Al alloys with Al contents of 15, 20, 25, 28, 30 and 35% Al prepared in the same study; some of the 20 and 30% Al alloys were additionally modified with 0.1% B, but this sample is the B-free binary Fe–30% Al. No other alloying element or deliberate solute/precipitate addition is reported, so there is no grain-size, solution or particle contribution to strength in the intended comparison to literature data.
processing: Alloys were prepared by standard induction melting in an alumina crucible under inert gas, followed by drop casting into a 25 mm diameter cylindrical copper mould, producing samples with grain size of the order of 0.25 mm. Cooling after solidification was sufficiently slow to allow a high degree of B2 order for Al-rich alloys and a good degree of DO3 order for alloys containing 25–30% Al, as confirmed later by strong superlattice spots and coarse DO3 domains in TEM. Compression specimens were cut by spark machining from the ingots either as 3 mm diameter cylinders or as 5 mm × 5 mm square cross-section bars, with height twice the diameter/width; flat surfaces were polished on 1500 grade abrasive paper before testing. The specimens were compressed at room temperature to a strain of 2–3% at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, with the compression axis always parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples. Following testing, thin foils for TEM were cut with a diamond saw from the centre of the deformed samples perpendicular to the stress axis and prepared by twin-jet electropolishing in 25% nitric acid in methanol at about 20 V and −30 °C.
microstructure: The slowly cooled Fe–30% Al is a weakly DO3-ordered alloy with a high degree of B2 order: the B2-ordered FeAl phase (ordered bcc) is well developed, while DO3 order is weak, appearing as fine DO3 domains or partial disorder. Prior to deformation the grain size is of the order of 0.25 mm. After room-temperature deformation to 2–3%, the substructure consists of superdislocations that are invariably composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials — perfect superdislocations of the B2 lattice but imperfect superdislocations of the DO3 lattice, which therefore trail APBII faults as they glide. Many of these dislocations are rather straight and lie in near-screw orientations; in addition there are numerous edge dislocation dipoles and dipole loops, observed as closely spaced parallel image pairs (marked d) at both low and high magnification. Because the APBI fault energy is sufficiently high at 30% Al, the two partials of the superdislocation remain closely coupled, so the parallel pairs imaged are short or long dipole dislocation pairs rather than separated partials. Reactions between dislocations produce stepped structures and further dislocation pairs that are reaction products, not the partials of the glissile superdislocations. A large number of fringes traversing the entire studied area are due to residual contrast of APBII fringes produced during deformation, because the moving pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials destroy some of the DO3 order. No precipitates are reported, and no four-partial (perfect DO3) superdislocations were observed in this material.
properties: Mechanical behaviour was assessed in room-temperature compression at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; the compression axis was parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples. For Fe–30% Al the yield strength lies at the plateau level of roughly 300–350 MPa that characterizes the 28–40% Al range after the sharp yield-stress maximum near 26% Al. The stress–strain response shows a smooth onset of plasticity, with no discrete yield point and slightly curved flow, and no linear stress–strain region. The work hardening rate measured as the secant over the 1–1.5% strain range reaches its peak of up to about 15 GPa near 30% Al, i.e. this composition sits at the sharp maximum of work hardening rate for binary Fe–Al alloys (peak found anywhere in the 26–29% Al range depending on strain range). Characterization was by transmission electron microscopy (JEOL 2010): thin foils electropolished in 25% nitric acid in methanol at ~20 V and −30 °C, with dislocations imaged in Bright Field and Weak Beam modes, planar (shear or thermal) faults imaged in various dark field modes, Burgers vectors identified by imaging with a variety of g vectors (generally in Bright Field), and ±g imaging pairs used to certify dipole configurations.
mechanisms: Slow cooling after solidification of the 25–30% Al alloys permits a high degree of B2 order and a good degree of DO3 order, so Fe–30% Al is weakly DO3-ordered while remaining well B2-ordered.

Because 30% Al lies in the ordered range, plasticity is carried by superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials — these are perfect superdislocations for the B2 lattice but imperfect superdislocations for the DO3 lattice, so they trail APBII faults as they glide.

The APBI fault energy at 30% Al is sufficiently high that the two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials of the superdislocation stay closely coupled; the parallel dislocation image pairs observed are therefore short or long dipole pairs, not separated partials.
Movement of the (1/2)⟨111⟩ partial pairs destroys part of the DO3 order during deformation, which is left visible as residual-contrast APBII fringes traversing the deformed areas.

Frequent reactions between superdislocations of different Burgers vectors produce stepped structures and straight paired dislocations; these pairs are reaction products and do not correspond to the partials of the glissile superdislocations.

The predominance of straight, near-screw dislocation segments in the ordered alloys is attributed to strong Peierls forces for compositions close to 25–30% Al (coinciding with, but not caused by, the elastic-anisotropy maximum), rather than to the elastic anisotropy itself.

Superdislocations gliding in screw orientations leave dipole debris (superdislocation dipoles) behind them and on meeting obstacles, and these stronger superdislocation dipole locks give the ordered state a higher work hardening rate than the single-dislocation dipoles of the disordered alloys.

For alloys near the work-hardening peak (28–30% Al) reactions of 1 1 1 superdislocations with different Burgers vectors produce pairs of sessile 1 0 0 edge dislocations on cube planes (locks) that prevent further room-temperature superdislocation motion, contributing to the high work hardening.
conclusions: Fe–30% Al belongs to the high-Al, ordered end of the alloy series in which the work hardening rate of polycrystalline Fe–Al peaks (maximum near 28% Al, in the 26–29% Al range). Room-temperature deformation to 2–3% in this weakly DO3-ordered, coarse-grained material proceeds exclusively by B2 superdislocations made of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials that leave numerous edge dipoles and loops, form straight near-screw segments, and react with each other into stepped structures and sessile reaction products. The work hardening of the ordered alloys is attributed to the presence of superdislocations, which produce stronger dipole locks than single dislocations, combined with the strong preference of dislocations to lie in screw orientations (linked to high Peierls forces near 25–30% Al rather than to the elastic anisotropy peak itself); the same composition range shows reactions of 1 1 1 dislocations into sessile 1 0 0 edge dislocations that may act as additional barriers. The high work hardening rate near 28% Al, over a range where the flow stress is relatively constant, is used to explain the small ductility maximum of about 5–6% observed near 28% Al. As a documentation sample, Fe–30% Al shows that the mobility of the (1/2)⟨111⟩ partial pairs destroys part of the DO3 order during straining, leaving residual APBII contrast fringes throughout the deformed area, and it provides no evidence for coupled four-partial perfect DO3 superdislocations.
unmapped: For Fe–30% Al the APBI fault energy is sufficiently high that the separation of the partials constituting the superdislocation is small; the parallel image pairs visible in the higher-magnification micrograph all correspond to short or long dipole dislocation pairs rather than separated partials.

Fringes traversing the deformed Fe–30% Al areas are due to residual contrast of APBII fringes produced during deformation of this weakly DO3-ordered material, because the pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials destroy this order during movement.

The sample is part of a wider comparison across Fe–Al alloys studied after the same 2–3% room-temperature straining, where disordered 15–20% Al alloys deform by single curved (1/2)⟨111⟩ dislocations that readily bow into edge as well as screw orientations, whereas DO3-ordered Fe–25% Al has APB energies too low to keep partials coupled so that single dislocations trail shear APB faults; Fe–30% Al represents the more strongly coupled, straight near-screw superdislocation regime shared with 28 and 35% Al.

About 0.1% B addition to Fe–Al alloys produces only a slight increase in flow stress and little consistent change in work hardening rate; this is reported for the alloy series and is not specific to the binary Fe–30% Al sample.
